title: The transparent eyeball
hook: Emerson, on a bare common at twilight, feels himself become nothing and see all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Whitman's leaf of grass, no less than the journeywork of the stars. Your line was journeywork of the stars. Today ends the week, with a man crossing a muddy field at dusk.

Snow puddles. A bare town common. Twilight, and a cloudy sky. Nothing special happening. Here's how Ralph Waldo Emerson describes it in his book Nature: "Crossing a bare common, in snow puddles, at twilight, under a clouded sky, without having in my thoughts any occurrence of special good fortune, I have enjoyed a perfect exhilaration. I am glad to the brink of fear." No mountaintop. No good news. Wet feet. A few sentences on, his thoughts gone to the woods, he reaches for a very strange picture.
screen: `SNOW PUDDLES AT TWILIGHT.` → `NO SPECIAL GOOD FORTUNE.` → `A PERFECT EXHILARATION.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "Standing on the bare ground, my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space, all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all". First, the ordinary setting. Emerson goes out of his way to say nothing lucky had happened. The joy comes from bare ground and open air, not from his day going well. Second, glad to the brink of fear. Pascal's spaces frightened him; Wordsworth's presence disturbed him with joy. Emerson's gladness comes right up to fear and stops there. Third, what disappears. Not Emerson himself: what vanishes is "mean egotism", the small, grasping self that keeps score. With that gone, "I am nothing; I see all". A transparent eye doesn't look at itself. It only lets the world through. Fourth, the week. Seven people, seven ways of looking. Pascal and the silent spaces. Kant's two things, above and within. Wordsworth's presence. Blake's world in a grain. Hopkins and a world charged. Whitman's grass, the journeywork of the stars. And Emerson, nothing, seeing all. Some of them name God, as Emerson does a few words later, calling himself "part or particle of God". Some leave the name out. Each stood still long enough for something to come through.
screen: `NO SPECIAL GOOD FORTUNE` · `GLAD TO THE BRINK OF FEAR` · `I AM NOTHING; I SEE ALL` · `A WEEK OF LOOKING UP` · then, large: `NOTHING, SEEING ALL.`

segments.voice: Stand still in an open space, a yard, a balcony, or a doorway with the sky in it, arms loose, and let the air touch your face. Let your attention go outward only: what you see, what you hear, what you feel on your skin. Each time a thought about yourself comes up, a plan, a worry, a score, notice it, and turn back to seeing.
mean egotism. Emerson's name for the small, grasping self that vanishes when nothing is left but seeing. Today's word.
Your line: nothing, seeing all. The small self steps aside, and the world comes through. A week of looking, complete.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often meet this passage from Nature as a description of awe outdoors, and some people on a personal spiritual path practice standing still in open spaces, attention turned outward, as a short daily discipline.

chat.says: What did Emerson mean when he said he became a 'transparent eye-ball'?
options: That his small, score-keeping self vanished, and he simply let the world through.
That he saw so clearly he could see through people and know their thoughts.
That he felt invisible and lonely, as if nobody on the common could see him.
